extracted.intended_audience: Citizens and voters of New York; readers engaged in the Constitutional ratification debate and those interested in federal constitutional design
extracted.subtask_description: Guiding principles and specific provisions for the proper scope, distribution, and organization of the federal judiciary under the proposed U.S. Constitution (as argued in Federalist Papers Nos. 80–81).

rubrics_metrics.name: Jurisdiction over cases arising under U.S. laws
rubrics_metrics.description: The judiciary authority of the Union ought to extend to all those which arise out of the laws of the United States, passed in pursuance of their just and constitutional powers of legislation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There must always be a constitutional method of giving efficacy to constitutional provisions; federal courts are necessary to enforce restrictions on state legislatures (e.g., prohibitions like emission of paper money) and to give uniform interpretation and effect to federal laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jurisdiction over cases arising under the Constitution and articles of Union
rubrics_metrics.description: The judiciary should extend to all those cases which concern the execution of the provisions expressly contained in the articles of Union (i.e., cases arising under the Constitution).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uniformity in interpretation of national laws requires federal courts; matters that stem directly from constitutional prohibitions or provisions (e.g., state actions forbidden by the Constitution) must be cognizable in national tribunals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jurisdiction where the United States is a party
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal courts should have cognizance of all those cases in which the United States are a party.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Controversies between the nation and its members or citizens can only be properly referred to national tribunals; any other plan would be contrary to reason, precedent, and decorum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jurisdiction over matters affecting the peace of the Confederacy
rubrics_metrics.description: The judiciary should extend to all those causes which involve the peace of the Confederacy, whether relating to intercourse between the United States and foreign nations, or between the States themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: National peace requires federal determination of cases involving foreigners or inter-state relations; a distinction between treaty/nations-law cases and municipal-law cases is impractical and unsafe—best to refer all cases involving foreigners or national questions to national tribunals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admiralty and maritime jurisdiction
rubrics_metrics.description: The federal judiciary should extend to all those causes which originate on the high seas, and are of admiralty or maritime jurisdiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maritime causes generally depend on the laws of nations and affect rights of foreigners, implicating public peace; admiralty jurisdiction is an appropriate federal subject and is already, under the Confederation, submitted to national jurisdiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jurisdiction where state tribunals cannot be impartial
rubrics_metrics.description: The judiciary should extend to all those cases in which the State tribunals cannot be supposed to be impartial and unbiased.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No one ought to be a judge in his own cause; when local attachments, state interests, prejudged laws, or personal bias make state courts unreliable (e.g., land claims under competing state grants), federal tribunals are the proper forum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coextensiveness of judicial and legislative authority
rubrics_metrics.description: The propriety of the judicial power of a government being coextensive with its legislative power: the judiciary must be as extensive as the legislation it enforces to secure uniform interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thirteen independent courts of final jurisdiction interpreting the same national laws would cause contradiction and confusion; uniformity demands national tribunals with authority to construe laws made under federal powers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equity jurisdiction alongside law jurisdiction
rubrics_metrics.description: The federal judiciary should include equitable as well as legal jurisdiction (i.e., jurisdiction in law and equity arising under the Constitution and laws of the United States).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many disputes involve fraud, trust, hardship, or hard bargains that require equitable relief; without equitable jurisdiction, federal courts could be unable to do justice in matters involving foreigners or agreements between parties under differing state grants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jurisdiction over treaties and diplomatic matters
rubrics_metrics.description: The judiciary should extend to treaties made under U.S. authority and to all cases affecting ambassadors, other public ministers, and consuls.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These matters are intimately connected with the preservation of national peace and respect for sovereigns; they belong properly to national tribunals rather than local courts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jurisdiction over controversies between States and between citizens of different States
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal courts should decide controversies to which the United States shall be a party; controversies between two or more States; between a State and citizens of another State; and between citizens of different States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such jurisdiction is essential to prevent interstate bickerings, territorial disputes, and to secure harmony—historical examples show the necessity of a neutral national forum (e.g., the Imperial Chamber example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Jurisdiction for citizens of same State claiming lands under different State grants
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal cognizance should extend to cases between citizens of the same State claiming lands under grants of different States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are specifically contemplated instances where state courts will often be biased due to state laws or sympathies; federal jurisdiction prevents local prejudice in matters implicating inter-state rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal judiciary as protector of privileges and immunities equality
rubrics_metrics.description: To secure the equal privileges and immunities of citizens of each State, their construction should be committed to a tribunal without local attachments—the national judiciary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A national tribunal, owing its existence to the Union and not tied to any State, is most likely to be impartial and to give full effect to these fundamental provisions against evasion and subterfuge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitation of Supreme Court original jurisdiction
rubrics_metrics.description: The Supreme Court is to be invested with original jurisdiction only in cases affecting ambassadors, other public ministers and consuls, and those in which a State shall be a party.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original jurisdiction over such rare and dignity-related cases is appropriate; most other federal causes should originate in inferior tribunals so the Supreme Court can function chiefly as an appellate body.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power to constitute inferior federal courts
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress should have the power to ordain and establish inferior courts to obviate the necessity of having recourse to the Supreme Court in every case of federal cognizance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This enables federal tribunals in States or larger districts to handle national matters locally; it prevents overburdening the Supreme Court and allows appeals to be circumscribed practically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasons against relying solely on State courts for federal causes
rubrics_metrics.description: The plan of delegating federal causes exclusively to existing State courts is objectionable because local spirit or inappropriate court constitutions may disqualify them from exercising national jurisdiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State judges holding office at pleasure or short terms may lack independence; confidence in subordinate tribunals should influence the ease or difficulty of appeals—over-reliance on state courts could necessitate wide avenues of appeal and attendant inconveniences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appellate jurisdiction both as to law and fact
rubrics_metrics.description: The Supreme Court's appellate jurisdiction should extend both as to law and fact (subject to exceptions and regulations by Congress).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This general grant allows revision in cases determinable under different modes (common law vs. civil law); in some civil-law-type cases (e.g., prize causes) re-examination of facts may be essential for public peace. Congress may regulate whether fact re-examination occurs and by what procedures (remand, new jury, issues out of Supreme Court).

rubrics_metrics.name: Appellate jurisdiction does not abolish trial by jury
rubrics_metrics.description: The appellate jurisdiction of the Supreme Court does not, in itself, abolish the trial by jury.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislature may provide that appeals to the Supreme Court do not permit re-examination of facts tried by juries, or permit second juries; appellate review can be structured so as not to supplant jury trials where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Congressional power to make exceptions and regulations to appellate jurisdiction
rubrics_metrics.description: The appellate jurisdiction of the Supreme Court shall be subject to such exceptions and regulations as Congress shall make.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This constitutional provision enables the national legislature to adapt appellate procedures (including limits on fact review) to preserve public justice, security, and trial-by-jury safeguards as circumstances require.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appellate review as record-based vs. fact re-examination
rubrics_metrics.description: Appellate courts may take cognizance of facts 'as they appear upon the record' and pronounce the law arising on them, without instituting a new inquiry into the facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In some jurisdictions appellate jurisdiction includes both fact and law in the sense of reviewing the record; where necessary, re-examination of fact may be accomplished by remand or by directed issues, but appellate correction need not always mean new trials of fact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial independence and tenure considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Judicial offices should be held during good behavior (not short, temporary legislative terms) to secure independence and avoid legislative interference in judicial decision-making.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judges selected for life-tenure (or during good behavior) will have the specialized legal knowledge and insulation from faction required to interpret laws impartially; vesting ultimate judicial power in a body chosen for limited periods would be less eligible and prone to partisan influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of district/circuit organization for efficient justice
rubrics_metrics.description: It may be expedient to divide the United States into several districts (four or five or half a dozen) and institute a federal court in each district, with judges holding circuits aided by State judges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such organization would permit justice to be administered with ease and dispatch, allow appeals to be circumscribed within a narrow compass, and serve practical convenience better than one federal court per State.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sovereign immunity of States absent explicit surrender
rubrics_metrics.description: It is inherent in the nature of sovereignty not to be amenable to the suit of an individual without its consent; States retain this immunity unless they clearly surrender it in the Constitution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggestions that assignment of public securities would permit suits against States in federal courts are unfounded unless the plan effects an alienation of state sovereignty; contracts between a sovereign and individuals are binding in conscience but do not necessarily create a compulsive right of action against the sovereign absent its consent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance appellate accessibility with confidence in subordinate tribunals
rubrics_metrics.description: The ease or difficulty of appeals should correspond to the confidence in subordinate tribunals; over-permissive appeals create public and private inconvenience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If subordinate federal or state tribunals are trusted, appeals can be more limited; if not, appeals must be broader. The power to constitute inferior courts and to regulate appellate paths should aim to minimize inconvenience while securing justice.
